title: AI for Modding
author: DerekPaxton
selftext:
I started as a modded. And quit my “grown up job” to go work on games full time because modding worked out well for me.

So modding is always near and dear to my heart and an important part of every professional game I’ve made over the last 15 years.

But I released my latest game a month ago and adopted a different strategy. No editor, nothing easy. Just an export of 30,000 files so modders can modify whatever they want.

It’s madness, totally overwhelming and borderline unusable. Except for AI. Instead of attempting to the millions of lines of export, modders throw it into the AI, tell it what they want and it finds the changes.

It’s a massive change both as how I works as a dev (just raw exports) and what modders are able to do.

We often talk about modding for game dev here, but the impact on modding is considerable too.

comments.author: General_Correct
comments.body: In gamedev a lot of QAs are still doing their work manually or ask developers to create tools for them. Gamedev seems to me the only industry that still is so heavily relying on manual and not automated QA. Of course there are several notable exceptions like Larian that have an increadible level of build autoamtions and autotests, but they basically develop very similar systems-based games. I strongly believe that a lot of QAs need to ahve better tools, that can be considered "tools for modding" it's just not every company has time and money for this and not every developer can do it. Average game dev programmer is much less capable than average corporate software developer unfortunately.
